block_title: What a reservoir-to-river hydraulic transition means
statement: Reservoirs and rivers differ systematically in longitudinal water-surface geometry: impounded reaches tend towards low longitudinal gradients, whereas free-flowing reaches maintain persistent downstream gradients controlled by discharge, channel geometry, roughness and backwater conditions.

closest_existing_study_quote: Moreover, the longitudinal profiles from SWOT revealed significant backwater effects at the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers.
what_is_established: Evidence confirms that reservoirs and impounded reaches exhibit flattened longitudinal water-surface gradients [doi:10.3390/w15112057, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0068186]. Conversely, free-flowing rivers maintain gradients influenced by discharge and backwater effects [doi:10.1029/2025gl115953, doi:10.3390/rs16214010]. These distinct hydraulic characterisations demonstrate systematic differences in longitudinal geometry between impounded and natural riverine systems.
what_remains_missing: While the evidence supports the general distinction between impounded and free-flowing reaches, it lacks a comprehensive, comparative analysis that explicitly quantifies the systematic differences in longitudinal geometry across a broad range of global river systems.

block_title: What a reservoir-to-river hydraulic transition means
statement: Dam removal, dam failure or rapid reservoir drawdown can produce an abrupt transition from impounded hydraulic conditions towards a channelised fluvial regime, expressed through changes in water-surface slope, velocity, shear stress, width and connectivity.
closest_existing_study_title: Influence of Small Dams on Downstream Channel Characteristics in Pennsylvania and Maryland: Implications for the Long‐Term Geomorphic Effects of Dam Removal1
closest_existing_study_quote: Thus, dam removal in streams similar to those of our study area should not result in significant long‐term geomorphic changes.
what_is_established: Dam removal and reservoir drawdown trigger transitions from impounded to channelised fluvial regimes, causing increased flow velocity [doi:10.22230/jem.2009v10n1a412], channel incision [doi:10.1029/2006wr005621, doi:10.1029/2003wr002940], and knickpoint development [doi:10.25675/3.026556]. These processes alter hydro-morphodynamics and sediment transport [doi:10.2110/jsr.2018.61], though some studies suggest long-term geomorphic impacts may be limited in specific contexts [doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2008.00263.x].
what_remains_missing: The evidence lacks a comprehensive characterisation of the generalisability of these geomorphic responses across diverse river systems and dam types. Further research is required to reconcile the conflicting findings regarding the significance of long-term geomorphic changes following dam removal.
